title: Duplicates and data quality
goal: Find repeated records and validate IDs, ranges, and allowed labels.
prerequisites: You can filter rows, convert values, and count missing entries.

cells.title: Find an exact repeated record
cells.explanation: `duplicated()` marks repeated rows. By default, the first occurrence is kept unmarked and later copies are marked True. With `keep=False`, every member of a repeated set is marked.
cells.code:
df = raw_students()
result = df.loc[df.duplicated(keep=False), ["Student_ID", "Name", "Score"]]
print(result)
print("Extra copies:", df.duplicated().sum())

questions.prompt: Why use keep=False when investigating duplicates?
questions.answer: It shows both the original row and its duplicate so we can compare them.

questions.prompt: How many displayed rows and how many extra copies will we see?
questions.answer: Two displayed rows for S003, but only one extra copy.

questions.prompt: Is a repeated name enough to identify a duplicate person?
questions.answer: No. Different people can share a name; use the intended record key and relevant fields.

cells.task: Remove exact duplicate rows and reset the index. Store the result in `result`.
cells.solution:
df = raw_students()
result = df.drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)
print(result[["Student_ID", "Name", "Score"]])
print("Rows:", len(result))
cells.solution_note: Twelve rows remain. Other data-quality problems are still present and need separate treatment.

check.prompt: What does duplicated() count by default here?
options: Every occurrence of a repeated row
Only repeated copies after the first
check.feedback: The default keep="first" leaves the first copy unmarked.

cells.solution_verify:
assert len(result) == 12
assert not result.duplicated().any()
assert result.index.tolist() == list(range(12))
cells.watch: A duplicate record and a missing value are different problems.
cells.takeaway: Inspect repeated records before removing them.

cells.title: A repeated ID is not always an exact duplicate
cells.explanation: `subset` lets you check only the columns that define a record key. Two rows can share an ID but disagree on a score. Keeping the last one is defensible only when a documented order says it is the latest record.
cells.code:
df = pd.DataFrame({"Student_ID": ["S001", "S001", "S002"], "Updated": ["2026-10-01", "2026-10-03", "2026-10-02"], "Score": [80, 88, 72]})
result = df.loc[df.duplicated(subset=["Student_ID"], keep=False)]
print(result)
print("Exact duplicates:", df.duplicated().sum())

questions.prompt: Which field is being treated as the record key?
Are the two S001 rows exact duplicates?
questions.answer: No. Their dates and scores differ.

questions.prompt: Why would dropping one row without a rule be risky?
questions.answer: We could discard the correct observation; the meaning of the records and update order matters.

cells.task: Assume the later Updated date is the authoritative revision. Parse Updated, sort chronologically, and keep the latest row per Student_ID. Store the retained rows in result, sorted by Student_ID in ascending order.
cells.hint: Date parsing is introduced in Module 13: use pd.to_datetime with format="%Y-%m-%d". Sort by Updated before drop_duplicates(subset="Student_ID", keep="last"), then sort the retained rows by Student_ID.
cells.solution:
df = pd.DataFrame({"Student_ID": ["S001", "S001", "S002"], "Updated": ["2026-10-01", "2026-10-03", "2026-10-02"], "Score": [80, 88, 72]})
df["Updated"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Updated"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
result = df.sort_values("Updated").drop_duplicates(subset="Student_ID", keep="last").sort_values("Student_ID")
print(result)
cells.solution_note: S001 keeps score 88 from October 3; S002 keeps 72. The decision follows the stated update policy.

check.prompt: Does keep="last" automatically know the newest date?
options: No; the row order must first match the date rule
Only when the ID is numeric
check.feedback: Last means last in the current row order.

cells.watch: In a transaction table, repeated student IDs may be expected; define what one row represents.
cells.takeaway: Choose a key and a documented conflict rule.

cells.title: Flag impossible values instead of hiding them
cells.explanation: Data can have the right type and still be invalid. If Attendance is a percentage, its allowed range is 0 through 100. A Boolean mask can create a review table before you decide how to repair the source.
cells.code:
df = raw_students()
invalid = ~df["Attendance"].between(0, 100)
result = df.loc[invalid, ["Student_ID", "Attendance"]]
print(result)

questions.prompt: What does the ~ symbol do to the range check?
questions.answer: It reverses True and False, so rows outside the range are selected.

questions.prompt: Why should we not automatically change 105 to 100?
questions.answer: We do not know the correct value. Clipping can hide a recording error and overstate attendance.

cells.task: Preserve the source Attendance values in Attendance_raw. Convert Attendance to a nullable numeric column and set its out-of-range values to missing. Store the affected rows in result with columns Student_ID, Attendance_raw, and Attendance.
cells.hint: Use a copy, `astype("Float64")`, and one `.loc[mask, column]` assignment.
cells.solution:
df = raw_students()
df["Attendance_raw"] = df["Attendance"]
df["Attendance"] = df["Attendance"].astype("Float64")
invalid = ~df["Attendance"].between(0, 100)
df.loc[invalid, "Attendance"] = pd.NA
result = df.loc[invalid, ["Student_ID", "Attendance_raw", "Attendance"]]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The original 105 is retained for follow-up. The cleaned measurement is marked unknown, not changed to a guessed value.

check.prompt: Is a numeric value always a valid measurement?
options: No, it must also satisfy the measurement rules
Only when it has a decimal point
check.feedback: Type validation and range validation check different things.

cells.watch: The allowed range comes from the meaning of the variable, not from pandas.
cells.takeaway: Validate values against explicit domain rules.

cells.title: Turn expectations into assertions
cells.explanation: An assertion stops execution if an expectation is false. It is useful for classroom checks and analysis pipelines. Validate identity, required values, and ranges separately so a failure has a clear meaning.
cells.code:
df = students()
assert df["Student_ID"].notna().all(), "A student ID is missing"
assert df["Student_ID"].is_unique, "Student IDs must be unique here"
assert df["Score"].between(0, 100).all(), "Score outside 0-100"
result = {"rows": len(df), "valid_ids": True, "valid_scores": True}
print(result)

questions.prompt: What happens if an assertion condition is False?
questions.answer: Python raises an AssertionError and stops the normal execution of the cell.

questions.prompt: Will these checks pass for students()?
questions.answer: Yes. The clean teaching table has 12 unique nonmissing IDs and scores within the allowed range.

questions.prompt: Why test missing IDs separately from uniqueness?
questions.answer: A column with one missing ID can still be unique; uniqueness alone does not require every ID to be present.

cells.task: Add checks requiring Campus to be RAK or Dubai and Attendance to be 0-100. Store the two Boolean results in a dictionary named result with keys campus_ok and attendance_ok.
cells.solution:
df = students()
campus_ok = df["Campus"].isin(["RAK", "Dubai"]).all()
attendance_ok = df["Attendance"].between(0, 100).all()
assert campus_ok, "Unexpected campus label"
assert attendance_ok, "Attendance outside 0-100"
result = {"campus_ok": bool(campus_ok), "attendance_ok": bool(attendance_ok)}
print(result)
cells.solution_note: Both checks are True for the clean table. Applying equivalent checks to raw data would expose problems that need review.

check.prompt: For a Boolean Series with no missing values, what does .all() require?
check.feedback: With no missing values, every tested value must be True. By default, .all() skips missing values. Validate required non-missing values separately, or explicitly treat missing checks as False.

cells.verify:
assert result["rows"] == 12
assert result["valid_ids"] is True
cells.watch: Python can disable assert statements in optimized runs; formal applications may need explicit validation errors.
cells.takeaway: Write data expectations as checks you can repeat.
